idea.body: A sequence is a list that follows a rule. An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount every term, like 3, 7, 11, 15, adding 4 each time. A geometric sequence multiplies by the same amount every term, like 2, 6, 18, 54, multiplying by 3 each time. Written recursively, a rule only says how to get the next term from the one before it. Written explicitly instead, a_n = a_1 + d(n - 1) for arithmetic, or a_n = a_1 times r^(n - 1) for geometric. Either explicit formula jumps straight to any term, no building up needed.

figure.alt: A row of boxes for the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15, each 4 more than the last.

workedExample.prompt:
A rover's battery charge starts at 80 percent and drops by 5 percent every hour.
What is the charge after 6 hours, as a_7?
steps: The charge starts at a_1 = 80 and drops by 5 every hour, so this is arithmetic with d = -5.
After 6 hours is term 7 (the first term is hour 0).
The charge is 50 percent after 6 hours.

figure.alt: A row of boxes for the battery charge, 80, 75, 70, 65, each 5 less than the last.

ways.name: The explicit formula
ways.when: Use this to jump straight to any term without building the sequence up.
steps: The sequence 3, 7, 11, 15 adds 4 each time, so d = 4.
ways.trap: Forgetting the (n - 1) and writing a_n = a_1 + d times n instead.

figure.alt: A row of five boxes labeled 3, 7, 11, 15, with 4 written between boxes.

ways.name: Build the sequence term by term
ways.when: Use this when the explicit formula is hard to spot or you only need the next few terms.
steps: The sequence starts at 5 and multiplies by 2 each time.
Each term is the one before it times 2.
ways.example: Start at 5, multiply by 2 each time. Find term 5.
ways.trap: Losing track of which term you are on or multiplying by the wrong factor.

ways.name: Spot the pattern from differences or ratios
ways.when: Use this to identify what kind of sequence you have from raw data.
steps: Constant second difference means quadratic growth.
ways.trap: Stopping after finding first differences and not recognizing when second differences are constant.
